newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour 20 points ahead in Reuters/NOP poll.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour 20 points ahead in Reuters/NOP poll.

text.p: Britain's Labour opposition has still not shed its image as the party of high taxes but this will not deter voters from electing it to office with a commanding lead over the Conservatives, a poll for Reuters showed on Tuesday.

The pre-election survey of 1,049 voters across Britain by research organisation NOP put support, among those expressing a preference, at 50 percent for Labour compared with 30 percent for the Conservatives.
The Liberal Democrats polled 14 percent and other parties six percent -- including two percent for the Referendum party of Sir James Goldsmith.
Labour leader Tony Blair will be concerned that voters are still suspicious of his party when it comes to tax despite his pledge not to raise income tax rates for five years if Labour wins power.
Thirty-two percent of those questioned felt total taxes would be higher under a Labour government compared with just 19 percent who felt they would pay more under the Conservatives.
The poll is the first of a series that NOP is conducting for Reuters in the run-up to the election, which must be held by May 22 but is widely expected to take place on May 1.
NOP conducted face-to-face interviews on Friday, February 21 with 1,049 voters in 51 parliamentary constituencies.

In terms of overall voting intentions, the results of the survey are in line with other opinion polls since the start of the year. These have shown Labour, which has been in opposition since 1979, ahead of the Conservatives by 15 to 25 percentage points.
All political parties tend to play down the significance of opinion polls, remembering how they failed to predict the Conservatives' victory at the 1992 general election.
Prime Minister John Major has been waiting in vain for Britain's robust economic recovery to revive his party's popularity.
NOP found the Conservatives came out ahead, marginally, on the critical question of who voters most trusted to run the economy. The Conservatives polled 32 percent against Labour's 30 percent.
